## 1. What you'll build, and why

Concept 33's backend works, but it's a stack machine: every value round-trips through memory. A
hot loop reloads its operands from the frame on every iteration. This concept fixes that — it keeps
values in **registers** — and it's the single biggest performance lever in the native backend.

You build it as a **ladder**, three rungs you can select and benchmark independently:

- **v0 stack** — spill every value to its frame slot (essentially concept 33). Correct, slow.
- **v1 linear-scan** — assign registers over each value's *live interval*; under pressure, spill
  the interval that ends latest.
- **v2 graph-colouring** — model interference as a graph and colour it (Chaitin–Briggs).

isel now emits over **virtual registers** — each SIL value becomes a `Virt v`, an abstract,
unlimited register — and the allocator's job is to map those onto the machine's real, finite
register file (or spill to memory when there aren't enough).

- **You implement:** `linscan` and `graphcolor` — the two classic allocation algorithms, the cores
  of the ladder.
- **Outcome:** all three rungs produce native binaries matching `swiftc`; the upper rungs run
  **~2.9× faster than stack** (measured), approaching our LLVM `-O` path.

> **New to register allocation?** A CPU has a fixed, small set of fast registers (here, the 31
> general ones). A program has unboundedly many *values*. Register allocation decides which values
> live in which registers at which times, and which must be "spilled" to slower memory when the
> registers run out. It's the difference between fast code and a glorified interpreter.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Virtual registers, a callee-saved pool, and "spill = your slot"

![Left: isel emits each SIL value as a virtual register; the allocator places it in a physical register or spills it. Linear-scan walks live intervals and spills the one ending latest; graph-colouring colours the interference graph. The pool is the 9 callee-saved registers (so allocated values survive calls for free); a spill just means "live in your own frame slot." Right: measured runtimes — each rung beats the last, graph-colour ~2.9× over stack, approaching the LLVM -O path.](figs/ladder.png)

Three design choices make this tractable (and they're the reason the code is short):

1. **The pool is `x19`–`x27` — the callee-saved registers.** AAPCS64 guarantees a callee preserves
   these across a call, so any value we place in one **automatically survives a `bl`**. We never
   have to model which registers a call clobbers — a notorious source of register-allocator bugs.
   The prologue saves (and the epilogue restores) exactly the callee-saved registers we used.
2. **`x9`–`x14` are reserved scratch.** When a value is spilled, the rewrite loads it into a
   scratch register right before the instruction and stores the result right after. The allocator
   never touches scratch, so spill code never conflicts with allocated values.
3. **A "spill" is free to express.** Every virtual register already owns a frame slot
   (`[sp, #16 + 8*v]`). So "spill v" just means "v lives in its slot" — no spill-slot allocation,
   no frame growth. The v0 stack rung is literally "spill everything."

### The IR you allocate over

This concept adds no syntax either — it changes what concept 33's isel *emits*. Its input and
output are both `arm64.ml`, so the recall is of the register side of that IR, not a grammar
(EBNF conventions: `[ x ]` optional, `{ x }` zero-or-more, `|` alternatives, quoted terminals):

```
reg        ::= "X" int | "SP" | "XZR" | "Virt" int         (* Virt: now live  <-- new *)
loc        ::= "Reg" int | "Spill"                         (*                 <-- new *)
strategy   ::= "Stack" | "Linscan" | "Graphcolor"          (*                 <-- new *)
assignment ::= { int "->" loc }        (* what your two holes produce, keyed by vreg *)
```

Nothing about the *instructions* changes — the same `mov`/`add`/`ldr`/`bl`/`ret` forms concept 33
introduced, only now with `Virt v` in their register positions. Two given helpers are the whole
interface to them:

| helper | what it gives you |
|---|---|
| `Arm64.reads_writes i` | the registers instruction `i` reads and the ones it writes |
| `Regalloc.map_regs g i` | `i` with `g` applied to every register operand |

`reads_writes` is what makes liveness possible without a case per opcode, and `map_regs` is what
makes the rewrite one line per instruction. The printer refuses a `Virt` that reaches it, so an
allocation that misses a value is a loud failure rather than bad code.

### Liveness and live intervals (given)

Both algorithms need to know **when each value is alive** — from its definition to its last use. We
compute this by classic backward dataflow: `live_in[i] = (live_out[i] \ defs[i]) ∪ uses[i]`,
iterated to a fixpoint over the control-flow graph (so loops are handled correctly — a value used
at the bottom of a loop is live through the whole body). From the per-instruction live sets we
derive each value's **interval** `[start, end]` — the span of instruction indices over which it's
live. Two values **interfere** when their intervals overlap: they can't share a register.

`liveness` and `intervals` are given; you consume their output.

### Linear-scan (v1) — your first hole

Poletto & Sarkar's algorithm is beautifully simple. Sort the intervals by **start** point, and
sweep left to right keeping an `active` set (the intervals currently holding a register), sorted by
**end** point:

- **Expire**: before placing the current interval, return to the free pool any active interval
  whose end has already passed.
- **Allocate**: if a register is free, take it.
- **Spill under pressure**: if none is free, look at the active interval that ends **latest**. If
  it ends *after* the current one, **steal its register** (it had the most still to lose) and spill
  *it* instead; otherwise spill the current interval. Spilling the longest-lived value frees a
  register for the longest stretch — the greedy choice that makes linear-scan competitive.

One pass, no graph. It's what LLVM's fast (`-O0`-ish) allocator and many JITs use.

### Graph-colouring (v2) — your second hole

The Chaitin–Briggs view: build the **interference graph** (a node per value, an edge between values
whose intervals overlap), and a valid allocation is a **K-colouring** (K = 9 registers). The
algorithm:

- **Simplify**: repeatedly remove a node with **degree < K** and push it on a stack. Such a node is
  *always* colourable once its neighbours are coloured (it has fewer neighbours than colours), so
  removing it can't hurt. When every remaining node has degree ≥ K, remove the **highest-degree**
  one as a *spill candidate* and push it too.
- **Select**: pop the stack, giving each node a colour (register) that **none of its already-coloured
  neighbours** took. If every colour is taken (a real spill), mark it `Spill`.

Graph-colouring finds register assignments linear-scan misses under high pressure, because it sees
the *global* conflict structure, not just a left-to-right sweep. On low-pressure code (most of our
corpus — a handful of live values, well under 9) the two **coincide**; they diverge when live
values exceed the pool, which is exactly where colouring's global view pays off.

### The rewrite and frame finalization (given)

Once you've produced an assignment (`vreg → Reg r | Spill`), the given `rewrite` walks the
instructions: a value in a register becomes that physical register; a spilled value is loaded into
scratch before the instruction and stored after. It also reports which callee-saved registers got
used. Then `finalize` builds the frame. The body's slot offsets were fixed at isel time, so
finalize only needs to know *how many* callee-saved registers to save on top of them:

```
sub  sp, sp, #16          ; room for the frame record
stp  x29, x30, [sp, #0]   ; save the caller's frame pointer and our return address
mov  x29, sp              ; x29 = the record (the AAPCS64 frame chain)
sub  sp, sp, #LOCALS      ; the value slots, then the used callee-saved registers
str  x19, [sp, #…]        ; one per callee-saved register the allocator handed out
```

and the epilogue reverses it before every `ret`. The record goes down **first**, at offset 0, and
that matters: `stp`/`ldp` take a 7-bit signed immediate scaled by 8 (−512…+504), so the shorter
`sub sp, #FRAME` / `stp x29, x30, [sp, #FRAME-16]` shape stops assembling once the frame passes
about half a kilobyte — which under this concept's default allocator a forty-`let` `main` reaches.
Pushing the record first keeps the pair at offset 0 whatever the frame size (and `sub`/`add sp`,
whose immediate is 12 bits, step a very large locals area down in chunks). It is the same prologue
concept 35 needs for a different reason: there, `x29` becomes the handle for reading arguments the
caller passed on the stack.

### The honest gap to LLVM

The bench shows graph-colour reaching ~45% of our LLVM `-O` path, not 100%. The reason is principled:
we lower the **raw `-Onone`** SIL, where *variables* live in `alloc_stack` memory; register
allocation only places the **temporaries** (literals, arithmetic results) in registers. LLVM (and a
full backend) runs **mem2reg** first to promote variables into SSA values, so *they* get registers
too. Promoting variables — running our own mem2reg (concept 16!) before isel and lowering the
resulting block-arguments — is the documented next step; this concept nails the allocator itself.

> Oracle: the LLVM AArch64 greedy allocator; Poletto & Sarkar 1999 (linear scan); Chaitin 1982 /
> Briggs 1994 (graph-colouring with optimistic spilling). The algorithms you write are the
> textbook ones, at teaching scale.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab   C=phase8-arm64-backend/34-register-allocation
make bench C=phase8-arm64-backend/34-register-allocation
```

Two holes, two cram files, and each runs its own rung — so you can finish linear scan and watch
exactly one of them go green while the other still reads `TODO`.

- **`tests/regalloc-linscan.t`** (`TODO(34a)`) builds fib, a loop and integer division
  `--regalloc=linscan` and runs them; then contrasts the rung with the given stack rung on the
  same program — fewer `ldr`/`str`, and the callee-saved pool `x19`–`x27` used where stack uses
  none. It prints `_fib`'s prologue whole, so the frame contract is visible rather than asserted,
  and ends on Backend B agreeing with Backend A.
- **`tests/regalloc-graphcolor.t`** (`TODO(34b)`) is the same shape for colouring, plus the two
  facts only it can check: that a plain `build --native` picks it (it is the default rung), and
  that a forty-`let` `main` — a frame past a kilobyte — still assembles, with no `stp`/`ldp` at a
  nonzero offset.
- **`tests/oracle.t`** asks swiftc every run: 26 programs, each compiled by `swiftc -Onone`, by
  Backend A and by Backend B under **all three rungs**, all run, stdout and exit code
  byte-identical. This is the test that matters most here, because a mis-allocated value is
  *silent* — the wrong register still holds a number and the program still prints one. Five of
  the programs are written for pressure (twelve live `let`s, ten loop-carried variables, six live
  temporaries in a body, a recursion holding values across its own call, and the forty-`let`
  main).
- **`tests/test_regalloc.ml`** pins what cram cannot see. Soundness is checked *directly against
  the interference relation*: no two vregs whose intervals overlap may share a register, on
  straight-line code and on a loop. Eviction gets its own cases on a **hand-built** instruction
  stream — fourteen simultaneously-live virtual registers, nine registers, so exactly five must
  spill — because raw SIL keeps variables in memory and a Swift program of this subset almost
  never puts more than nine *temporaries* in flight at once.

Reading the report: an untouched hole shows as `TODO … not started`. `oracle.t` and the alcotest
suite show `FAIL` rather than `TODO` from the start, because their given-code cases (the front
end's multi-line literal, the stack rung, the frame shape) pass before you write a line.

## 5. Benchmark it

`bench/` compiles `hotloop`/`collatz`/`fibloop` with each rung plus the LLVM `-O` path, verifies
the outputs agree, and times them. Measured: **graph-colour ≈ 2.9× faster than stack (geomean)**,
2.3–4.3× per program, reaching ~45% of the LLVM path. Linear-scan ties graph-colour here (low
pressure). Report it honestly: the upper rungs win big over stack; the remaining gap to LLVM is the
in-memory variables, not the allocator.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Promote variables (mem2reg → SSA → φ-elimination).** Run concept 16's mem2reg before isel so
   variables become SSA values; lower block-arguments by inserting parallel copies on edges. Now
   the allocator can keep *variables* in registers — this is the single change that closes most of
   the gap to LLVM.
2. **Live-range splitting & spill-cost.** Instead of spilling a whole interval, split it so the
   hot part stays in a register. Weight spill choices by use-frequency (a value used in a loop is
   expensive to spill).
3. **Coalescing.** Eliminate a `mov xa, xb` by giving both the same register when they don't
   interfere (move-related coalescing) — Briggs/George conservative coalescing.
4. **Caller-saved registers too.** Add `x9`–`x15` to the pool for values *not* live across a call;
   model call-clobbers in the interference graph. More registers, more pressure relief.
5. **Better pressure test.** Construct a function with > 9 simultaneously-live values and show
   graph-colour spilling *less* than linear-scan — the case where they diverge.

## 7. Recap & what's next

Register allocation maps unlimited virtual registers onto a finite register file. The ladder —
**stack → linear-scan → graph-colouring** — climbs from "spill everything" to "keep what fits,"
each rung correct and each faster, the top ~2.9× over the bottom. The callee-saved pool makes calls
free; the per-value slot makes spilling trivial; liveness and intervals drive both algorithms.

Next, **35-mc-abi** — the full AAPCS64 / Apple ABI (real stack frames, argument passing beyond
eight registers, struct returns, `as`/`ld` details) — then **36-peephole-sched** (peephole cleanup
+ instruction scheduling, which would delete that redundant `str`/`ldr` pair you can see in the
asm) and **37-debug-info** (a DWARF-lite line table) to reach **M8-core**.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

```ocaml
(* 34a — linear scan *)
let linscan (instrs : Arm64.instr array) : (int, loc) Hashtbl.t =
  let assign = Hashtbl.create 32 in
  let ivs = List.sort (fun (_,(s1,_)) (_,(s2,_)) -> compare s1 s2)
              (intervals instrs (liveness instrs)) in
  let free = ref pool and active = ref [] in            (* active = (vreg,end,reg), by end *)
  let expire start =
    let keep, gone = List.partition (fun (_,e,_) -> e >= start) !active in
    List.iter (fun (_,_,r) -> free := r :: !free) gone; active := keep in
  List.iter (fun (v,(s,e)) ->
    expire s;
    match !free with
    | r :: rest -> free := rest; Hashtbl.replace assign v (Reg r);
        active := List.sort (fun (_,e1,_) (_,e2,_) -> compare e1 e2) ((v,e,r) :: !active)
    | [] ->
        let (lv,le,lr) = List.fold_left (fun a x ->
            if (let (_,e,_)=x in e) > (let (_,e2,_)=a in e2) then x else a)
            (List.hd !active) (List.tl !active) in
        if le > e then begin
          Hashtbl.replace assign lv Spill; Hashtbl.replace assign v (Reg lr);
          active := List.sort (fun (_,e1,_) (_,e2,_) -> compare e1 e2)
                      ((v,e,lr) :: List.filter (fun (vv,_,_) -> vv <> lv) !active)
        end else Hashtbl.replace assign v Spill) ivs;
  assign

(* 34b — graph colouring *)
let graphcolor (instrs : Arm64.instr array) : (int, loc) Hashtbl.t =
  let assign = Hashtbl.create 32 in
  let ivs = intervals instrs (liveness instrs) in
  let nodes = List.map fst ivs in
  let span = Hashtbl.create 32 in List.iter (fun (v,se) -> Hashtbl.replace span v se) ivs;
  let overlap (s1,e1) (s2,e2) = s1 <= e2 && s2 <= e1 in
  let adj = Hashtbl.create 32 in
  List.iter (fun v -> Hashtbl.replace adj v (Hashtbl.create 8)) nodes;
  let rec pairs = function [] | [_] -> () | a :: rest ->
    List.iter (fun b -> if overlap (Hashtbl.find span a) (Hashtbl.find span b) then (
        Hashtbl.replace (Hashtbl.find adj a) b (); Hashtbl.replace (Hashtbl.find adj b) a ())) rest;
    pairs rest in
  pairs nodes;
  let deg v rm =
    Hashtbl.fold
      (fun u () a -> if Hashtbl.mem rm u then a else a + 1)
      (Hashtbl.find adj v) 0
  in
  let removed = Hashtbl.create 32 and stack = ref [] in
  let remaining () = List.filter (fun v -> not (Hashtbl.mem removed v)) nodes in
  while remaining () <> [] do
    let rem = remaining () in
    let pick = match List.filter (fun v -> deg v removed < k) rem with v :: _ -> v
      | [] ->
          List.fold_left
            (fun a v -> if deg v removed > deg a removed then v else a)
            (List.hd rem) (List.tl rem)
    in
    Hashtbl.replace removed pick (); stack := pick :: !stack
  done;
  List.iter (fun v ->
    let used =
      Hashtbl.fold
        (fun u () a ->
          match Hashtbl.find_opt assign u with Some (Reg r) -> r :: a | _ -> a)
                 (Hashtbl.find adj v) [] in
    match List.filter (fun r -> not (List.mem r used)) pool with
    | r :: _ -> Hashtbl.replace assign v (Reg r) | [] -> Hashtbl.replace assign v Spill) !stack;
  assign
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — promote variables (the big one)
Before isel, run `Opt`'s mem2reg (concept 16) on the SIL. Now variables are SSA values flowing
through block arguments instead of `alloc_stack` loads/stores. In isel, lower a block argument to a
virtual register, and on each `Br (n, [a0;…])` to a block with parameters `[p0;…]`, emit moves
`p_i := a_i` *before* the branch (out-of-SSA / φ-elimination; use a temp for the rare cyclic case).
The allocator is unchanged — but now it sees the variables, so they get registers, and the gap to
LLVM mostly closes. This is why concept 16's block-argument SSA was worth building.

### 2 — live-range splitting & spill cost
Give each interval a *weight* = number of uses (×10 per loop nesting level). When you must spill,
spill the lowest weight-per-unit-length, not just the latest-ending. Splitting: when an interval
spans a region of high pressure, cut it into two (with a store/load at the cut) so only the cold
half spills.

### 3 — coalescing
A `mov xa, xb` where `a` and `b` don't interfere can be removed by allocating both to the same
register. Merge their interference nodes (conservatively — Briggs: only if the merged node has
< K neighbours of degree ≥ K) before colouring. Removes the parameter-shuffle `mov`s and many
SSA-elimination copies.

### 4 — caller-saved too
Add `x9`–`x15` to the pool, but only for values **not live across any `bl`**. Compute "crosses a
call" per interval; such intervals may use only callee-saved registers (or spill). More pool, less
spilling on call-free stretches — at the cost of modelling the call boundary.

### 5 — a divergence test
`let`-bind a dozen values all used together in one expression: their intervals all overlap, so > 9
interfere. Linear-scan (sweeping by start) spills whatever's active when it runs out; graph-colour,
seeing the full clique, spills the minimum. Count spills under each — graph-colour wins, the textbook
reason it exists.
```
